one_liner: Closed-source TU Munich research SQL database (HyPer successor) that runs ClickBench about 2.4x faster than ClickHouse on one node.
what_it_does: Umbra is a relational database from TU Munich's HyPer group. It is designed to give in-memory speed on the cached working set and fall back to SSD when data does not fit in RAM. It is a server, not a library. The umbradb/umbra Docker image starts a PostgreSQL-wire-compatible server, which Docker Hub calls a drop-in replacement for PostgreSQL, and also ships an umbra-sql command-line shell. Queries use the PostgreSQL SQL dialect, and the engine source is not published.
how_it_is_fast: Umbra compiles each query into code organised around the data flow. It uses its own lightweight intermediate representation (IR), generates machine code directly so execution starts almost immediately (the 'Flying Start' backend, with 'FireARM' for AArch64), and hands only long-running pipeline steps to the LLVM optimizing compiler (adaptive compilation). Work is spread across cores with morsel-driven parallelism. Storage sits on a buffer manager derived from LeanStore with variable-size pages (64 KiB minimum, power-of-two size classes), pointer swizzling and optimistic versioned latches, and the CIDR 2020 paper measures its overhead at under 6% on average versus flat memory-mapped tables. Strings use 16-byte headers that store strings of 12 bytes or fewer inline and keep a 4-byte prefix for longer ones.
when_to_use: Single-node ad-hoc analytical SQL over a wide table of about 100M rows (filtered counts, GROUP BY, COUNT(DISTINCT), LIKE '%x%' scans, top-N) when hot-query latency matters: on ClickBench it beats ClickHouse on 40 of 43 queries, often by 2-18x.
Machines with plenty of RAM: on c6a.metal it completes all 43 queries with a 3.8s hot sum and no concurrent-test errors.
Loading Parquet into a compressed table: ClickBench ingests the 14 GB hits.parquet through the umbra.parquetview table function in 163s and stores it in 8.3 GB with zstd (ClickHouse: 182s, 9.4 GB).
Join-heavy analytical SQL: the CIDR 2020 paper reports geometric-mean speedups of 3.0x over HyPer and 4.6x over MonetDB on the Join Order Benchmark (2.3x over MonetDB on TPC-H SF10).
Research or benchmarking where you want a state-of-the-art compiled engine as a reference point behind a PostgreSQL endpoint and running a Docker container is fine.
when_not_to_use: Production use: the license in the Docker image says the software is 'intended strictly for internal evaluation and review purposes and not for production purposes'. The commercial product from the same group is CedarDB.

Small-memory machines: in the 2026-09-18 ClickBench run, 14 of 43 queries failed on c6a.large with 'ERROR: unable to allocate memory' (mostly COUNT(DISTINCT) and big GROUP BYs), and 17 failed on t3a.small. ClickHouse finished all 43 on c6a.large. Earlier 16 GB runs also failed during data load.

Many concurrent clients on mid-size boxes: in ClickBench's 10-connection, 600-second test, 54.7% of attempted queries errored on c6a.4xlarge (58.8% on c8g.4xlarge; ClickHouse 0.1%). The log does not say why.
Anything that needs source code, patches, audits, embedding in-process or a distributed or replicated cluster: it is a proprietary, binary-only, single-node server.
ClickHouse-specific workloads: it speaks PostgreSQL SQL and wire protocol, not ClickHouse SQL, HTTP or native protocol, and has no MergeTree-style engines.

integration.form: Prebuilt Linux Docker image (umbradb/umbra) running a PostgreSQL-wire server plus the umbra-sql CLI; no library or source
integration.dependencies: Docker; any PostgreSQL client (psql, libpq, JDBC, etc.)
integration.min_toolchain: not applicable (prebuilt binary); host kernel and Docker version requirements not documented
integration.platforms: linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 images (arm64 since the 26.01 tag, January 2026; earlier tags amd64 only); ClickBench ran it on AMD c6a/c7a and Graviton c8g
integration.thread_safety: Multi-client server with ACID transactions via MVCC (per umbra-db.com); ClickBench's concurrent test shows high error rates under memory pressure
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it can replace ClickHouse only as a single-node analytical SQL endpoint. Clients, SQL dialect and schemas (ClickHouse table engines and ORDER BY keys) have to be ported to PostgreSQL equivalents.

gotchas: In May 2026 the ClickBench maintainer found that Umbra silently returns a NULL row for unimplemented functions (e.g. regexp_substr), with no error, so a query can look like a microsecond-fast success. The note was removed in the 26.09 update, and whether it was fixed is not documented.

When memory ran out during bulk load, the load transaction errored partway through but the harness carried on, leaving a partial table that gave implausibly fast timings. Check row counts after loading.

The ClickBench maintainer found memory settings hardcoded in the binary (shared_buffers 128MB, work_mem 4MB): 'SET work_mem' is rejected and ALTER SYSTEM is 'not implemented yet'. The only runtime knob in ClickBench's scripts is the ASYNCIO=0 environment variable.
It needs raised container limits: Docker Hub's quick-start sets nofile=1048576 and memlock=8 GiB, and ClickBench runs it --privileged with unlimited memlock.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Umbra for the fastest single-node SQL engine behind a PostgreSQL endpoint when an evaluation-only, closed-source license is acceptable. Pick chDB (in-process ClickHouse for Python) or Bodo (compiled Python DataFrames) when you need open source, production use, or execution inside a Python process.
verified_claims_summary: ClickBench's GitHub Actions automation ran the vendor's umbradb/umbra:26.09 image (submitted in PR #2066 by Umbra team member Tobias Schmidt) on one AWS c6a.4xlarge over the 100M-row hits table, untuned. Summing each query's best hot run over 43 queries gives 7.41s for Umbra, 18.03s for ClickHouse (2026-09-26, about 2.4x) and 26.25s for DuckDB (2026-05-11); cold sums are 47.3s vs 114.2s. ClickHouse wins only Q2 hot (1 ms vs 4 ms), and compiler and flags are unknown because only the binary is tested.
status_note: Actively released, with roughly monthly Docker tags from 25.01 to 26.09 (pushed 2026-09-16). It is a research project whose license allows only internal evaluation, so use it as a reference point and look at CedarDB for a supported product.
